## The question

[How to find the derivative of a function involving a square root more efficiently?](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/5148451/how-to-find-the-derivative-of-a-function-involving-a-square-root-more-efficientl), asked by [Fr2026](https://math.stackexchange.com/users/1775578/fr2026) on Mathematics Stack Exchange (2026-09-02; [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)):

> Today I came across a geometry question:
>
> > Quadrilateral $ABCD$ is a square and there are two moving points, $E$ on $AB$ and $F$ on $BC$, and $AE=BF$, $AB=1$ at all times.  
> Find the minimum of $AF+CE$.
> >
> >[![A square, ABCD, with points E and F on edges AB and BC respectively.  Lines AF and CE are also marked][q-1]][q-1]
>
> It's not very difficult to solve it, actually there is a clever way in geometry to solve this kind of problem. But I found that if I use the derivative to solve it, I will get a long function:
>
> $$f(x)=\sqrt{x^{2}+1^{2}}+\sqrt{(1-x)^{2}+1^{2}}$$
>
> There are many functions involving a square root, but working them out is difficult, so I want to find a more efficient way to work them out.
>
> Here is my way, but I'm not sure it is right:
>
> If $\sqrt{a}>\sqrt{b}$ ($a>0$, $b>0$), then $a>b$. So when $a$ attains its minimum, the value of $\sqrt{a}$ is also minimized. So maybe $\arg \min a(x)+b(x)=\arg \min \sqrt{a(x)}+\sqrt{b(x)}$,so my method is let $g(x)=a(x)+b(x)$ and get the minimum $f_{min}=f(g^{-1}_{min})$.\
> Let
>
> $$g(x)=x^{2}+1^{2}+(1-x)^{2}+1^{2}=2x^{2}-2x+3$$
>
> Then
>
> $$g'(x)=4x-2$$
> $$4x-2=0$$
> $$x=0.5$$
>
> So
>
> $$f_\textrm{min}=\sqrt{0.5^{2}+1^{2}}+\sqrt{(1-0.5)^{2}+1^{2}}=\sqrt{5}$$
>
> The minimum of $AF+CE$ is $\sqrt{5}$.
>
> Is my way to solve this problem right?
>
>
>   [q-1]: 7mmXy7eK.png
:::

The reason that $g(x)$ and $F(x) = g(x)^2$ have critical points at the same places is that 
$$F'(x) = \frac{d}{dx}\left[g(x)^2\right] = 2g(x) g'(x)$$
So $F'(x) = 0$ iff $g(x) = 0$ or $g'(x) = 0$. This is handy when $g$ is the square root of another function, because then we can square it away, and focus on minimizing the radicand.

But given two functions $g$ and $h$, the sums $f(x) = g(x) + h(x)$ and $F(x) = g(x)^2 + h(x)^2$ need not have this relation. This time,
$$F'(x) = 2 g(x) g'(x) + 2h(x) h'(x)$$
and this is not a multiple of $f'(x) = g'(x) + h'(x)$. 

For a counterexample, try $g(x) = x$ and $h(x) = x^2$. Then $f(x) = x + x^2$ has its minimum at $x=-\frac{1}{2}$, because $f'(x) = 1+2x$.
But $F(x) = x^2 + x^4$ has its minimum at $x=0$, because $F'(x) = 2x + 4x^3 = 2x(1+2x^2)$.

The derivative calculus with the square roots is not that bad in this case. For $f(x) = \sqrt{x^2+1} + \sqrt{(1-x)^2 + 1}$, we have
$$\begin{aligned}
  f'(x) &= \frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2+1}} + \frac{x-1}{\sqrt{(1-x)^2 + 1}}
\\&= \frac{x\sqrt{(1-x)^2 + 1} + (x-1)\sqrt{x^2+1}}{\sqrt{x^2+1}\sqrt{(1-x)^2 + 1}}
\end{aligned}$$
If $f'(x) = 0$, then the numerator of $f'(x) = 0$ too, which means that
$$\begin{aligned}
  x\sqrt{(1-x)^2 + 1} = -(x-1)\sqrt{x^2+1}
\end{aligned}$$
Squaring both sides, we have
$$\begin{aligned}
  x^2\left((1-x)^2 + 1\right) &= (x-1)^2\left(x^2+1\right) \\
\implies
  x^2(x^2-2x+2) &= (x^2-2x+1)(x^2+1) \\
\implies
  x^4 - 2x^3 + 2x^2 &= x^4 - 2x^3 + 2x^2 -2x + 1 \\
\implies 
  0 &= 1-2x \implies x = \frac{1}{2}
\end{aligned}$$
It would be messier if we broke the symmetry, as David points out. But squaring both terms will not produce the correct solution.
